spoiler_text.text:
We open at the Dashwood estate. Middle daughter Marianne Dashwood (Esmé Creed-Miles) sits in the grass, taking in nature. Hearing horses in the distance, she runs to a carriage where she receives mail; their late father’s last will and testament. Returning to the house, she meets with her sisters; eldest Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and youngest Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach). Marianne is afraid to open it, so Elinor does, telling her sisters that whatever it says “We will face it together.”

Later, the three girls sit with their mother Mrs. Dashwood (Caitriona Balfe) as they absorb the truth of the document. Their father had been married before and by law, the estate will go to his son, John Dashwood (Tom Brooke). The family bemoans how the law works, but their mother says they will make do with their inheritance of five thousand pounds. Elinor corrects her mother, saying their father only left them five hundred. Marianne for her part cannot understand why John needs the place, as he is already wealthy with a house in London. They soon see John is arriving, and their mother instructs them to be civil as they are family, reminding her girls that “Wealth has nothing to do with happiness” as their father chose to marry her even though she didn’t have a dowry.

John arrives with his wife Fanny (Stacy Martin) and his young son. Fanny tells her son he will be the lord of the estate one day, but he has no interest in it and would like to return home. Mrs. Dashwood extends her condolences to John, saying his father was a good man. Fanny rudely interrupts, asking for a tour of the grounds, thinking the second family of Dashwood Sr. is beneath her.

The two families try to coexist as best as possible, but soon learn that Fanny’s older brother Edward Ferrars (George Mckay) will be staying with them as well.

John had been asked by his dying father to take care of his wife and his half sisters but Fanny browbeats him into giving them less, from a thousand pounds to three hundred, and a hundred pound a year annuity for Mrs. Dashwood given she will probably never remarry. As Fanny strangles the financial future of the Dashwood family, she looks over fine silver and all the possessions of the house that are now by extension, hers.

Marianne sadly packs up the books, telling Elinor that Fanny will probably just sell them, as she doubts she even reads. Elinor tells her that they must be civil. Marianne asks Elinor to admit she hates Fanny too, but Elinor replies they do not have the financial security to be mean even if Fanny deserves it.

Outside, they hear an arriving visitor and realize it is Edward. They both look outside but as he turns, they crouch down. Marianne asks Elinor to go meet him, as she fears he will be just as awful as Fanny is.

Elinor goes downstairs and meets Edward. For both, it is love at first glance. They bow to each other and introduce themselves. Edward hears Marianne playing the piano and comments on it, and Elinor tells him she hopes he likes music as Marianne plays often. They hear her cry out, obviously still mourning losing her home. Fanny arrives and seeing the moment between the two, quickly ushers him away, wishing nothing more than to be rid of the Dashwood’s.

Margaret spends time tending to Edward’s horse and takes in the forested grounds, knowing she will not know them for much longer.

Some time later, Elinor collects Margaret for her to continue her studies, which she is not interested in, causing them to struggle in a half serious fight. Edward comes across the two, and offers a walk. Elinor changes her tune immediately and has Margaret come with them. As they walk, he lightly flirts with Elinor and charms her younger sister with his playfulness, which only makes Elinor smile more.

Taking some time alone, they skip stones at a nearby pond. Elinor asks about his life, his family. Edward says his mother has great ambition for him, to be in parliament perhaps. However he has little ambition. When Elinor presses him on having something to work towards, Edward says perhaps a life in the Clergy, a small parish, and a family to love.

“I wish as everyone else to be happy,” Edward says.

“And what, pray tell, would make you happy?” Elinor asks him with a glance.

Edward holds out his hand, as if to take hers. Taken aback, she gently offers him another stone to skip.

That night, Edward poses for her, allowing Elinor to draw him. Her mother notes their mutual affection, especially of her daughter to Edward. “Has she once this few weeks ever left his side?”

Putting the complete drawing in the dresser, Elinor gets ready for bed with Marianne. They talk of Edward and it is here we see the difference between the two sisters. Marianne is guided by passion while Elinor is more modest. Marianne tells her sister that if she loves Edward, she will endeavor to love him too. Elinor uses guarded language to hide her growing feelings and notes that Edward is shy too. Marianne tells Elinor that the man who loves her must “burn with it.” Elinor wonders if a man that her sister desires even exists. “I require so much,” Marianne says, which makes Elinor laugh.

The following day, Marianne walks the grounds. As it begins to rain, she races through the forest, into the path of a man on horseback, startling the horse. As the man dismounts the horse, Marianne briefly looks at him and runs off laughing. The man, however, is transfixed by her beauty and fiery spirit. The man is Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum).

Elinor is in the study, looking over papers, distressed. Edward enters the room, having sent another failed query for housing. The Dashwood family is now unable to find a place close and cheap enough for them to survive. Elinor thanks Edward for all his help. Edward notes if he could, he would conspire to keep Elinor and her family at the estate, his hand so close to hers. Before he can say more, Fanny arrives and says a visitor has arrived to see them all. Elinor goes to meet them, with Edward following, only for Fanny to stop him. “Are you a Dashwood now too?” Fanny says coldly, obviously seeing their affection and doing everything to snuff it out for good.

The visitor is Mrs. Jennings (Fiona Shaw), a distant relative of the Dashwood family, who has heard of their situation, and has come to offer what assistance she can. She tells them that her son in law Sir John Middleton (Turlough Convery) has an unused cottage estate that she can convince him to rent at a low price, even though as Elinor notes it is quite further than they planned to relocate to. Mrs. Jennings tells the group that she was escorted by Colonel Brandon and notes he lives near them and is a wealthy man.

That night at dinner, Marianne asks Mrs. Jennings about Colonel Brandon. Meanwhile, Fanny is indirectly rude to Elinor, implying she is after Edward for his money since she no longer has any of her own. Having enough of the snide remarks, Mrs. Dashwood tells Mrs. Jennings she will accept her offer of the cottage rental and tells John Dashwood they will leave soon. John offers a final gift, against his wife’s objections, trying to honor his father’s wishes.

The next morning as the Dashwood girls are ready to leave, Elinor shares a conversation with Edward. Edward notes she must be sad leaving her home, but Elinor says she is ultimately happy most wherever her family is. Edward seemingly is about to propose, but then awkwardly asks to escort her outside. He then asks to call on her when she is settled in her new home, only to correct himself and say he meant her entire family. Elinor says of course, and as she leaves Edward winces, realizing he messed up.

As the Dashwood’s enter the carriage to leave, John tries to hand over a statue as a final gift, only to be stopped by his wife who doesn’t want to give them any more help. The Dashwood women depart, Elinor only looking at Edward as they leave.

After several days of travel, they make it to the cottage in Barton. While relatively large, it is still a downgrade from the mansion estate they were accustomed to. Mrs. Dashwood dryly jokes at least Fanny doesn’t live with them. In time, they settle in and make it home.

The Dashwood family attends a dinner with Mrs. Jennings and her son in law Sir John who is a boisterous, loud, but ultimately kind man. Sir John has a quiet, timid wife in Lady Middleton (Chloe Pirrie) who is seemingly obsessed with the weather. Also attending the dinner is Colonel Brandon who Marianne talks to. Marianne asks him about art, dancing, and museums, which she is passionate about. Brandon does not care for them much and tells her most people use their interests as a way to show off to people, and that he is at least passionate about not being insincere. Marianne counters that a man should at least PRETEND to be passionate about something, lest he is considered to be dull, which startles her mother with her boldness.

Later, Marianne plays the piano, with Brandon watching with rapt attention. Mrs. Jennings asks if he likes her playing. Brandon says he is paying Marianne the compliment by his attentiveness which makes Mrs. Jennings laugh. Marianne asks if he is a fan of music. Brandon says he was once and perhaps could be again, subtly commenting on how he likes how she plays.

The next day, Elinor sits in the kitchen and writes to Edward. Sir John arrives, bringing them fresh meat from his hunts, wanting to be sure they are well fed. He also brings them their mail, though tells Elinor there is no letter from Edward yet, but he will check for her daily, having heard of her affections of him from Mrs. Jennings.

Margaret and Marianne pick berries near the shoreline. Margaret notes that since she most likely will not have any money and skills of her own, she desires to marry a rich man, which makes her sister chuckle. They reach the beach, only for Marianne to twist her ankle badly at the water. Margaret runs to get help, and sees a nearby man on horseback. The man, John Willoughby (Frank Dillane) carries Marianne in his arms back to his horse.

Margaret returns to the house to tell her mother and Elinor that Marianne is hurt but a gentleman came to their rescue. Willoughby carries Marianne inside and tells the family that her ankle is thankfully not broken, but Marianne will need to rest it all the same. Mrs. Dashwood offers to let himself dry out from the rain, but Willoughby refuses. He does request to come by and check on Marianne the next day. As he departs, Marianne is overcome with emotion, having been immediately charmed by Willoughby, and her family joining in her happiness.

The next day, Marianne awkwardly has tea with Brandon, having heard of her accident. As he tries to confide in his relief to her health, Willoughby arrives with Sir John. Brandon sees Willoughby and it is clear he has issues with the man. As he wishes Marianne a quick recovery, Willoughby interrupts him, before Brandon repeats himself and departs, Elinor seeing and recognizing his quiet, restrained affection for Marianne. Willoughby mocks his dour nature. Sir John says he has decided to have a party, with lots of dancing. Marianne asks Willoughby if he loves dancing, and he replies that he does.

At Sir John’s party, there is much dancing and enjoyment. Willoughby dances with Marianne while Elinor and Brandon watch. Brandon tells Elinor her sister looks happy, to which Elinor says “excessively so.” Brandon asks if there is such a limit on happiness. Elinor tells him that Marianne’s emotions are an open secret and she lets everyone know how she feels. Brandon tells Elinor that he would not change a single thing about Marianne. “Such spirit is all too rare,” Brandon says. He watches as Willoughby picks Marianne up and swings her around the dance floor, making him jealous.

On a stairwell, Willoughby and Marianne talk of London and how they will dance together there in front of everybody. As they return to the party, they see Brandon hastily leave. Willoughby, with a touch of rudeness, says that Brandon is a man, “Everybody praises, but no one likes.”

Willoughby and Marianne spend more time together. Marianne reads to him and while she plays piano, they sing together. When she takes a bath that night, she sings the song they sang, thinking of him.

The next morning, Elinor sees Marianne on a horse. Initially believing Sir John had given it to her, Marianne tells her family it was a gift by Willoughby. Elinor balks, noting the cost and upkeep to have it. Marianne tells her sister to calm down and be happy for her. As she rides off on the horse, Mrs. Dashwood tells Elinor not to worry as Willoughby has requested a private audience with Marianne and thus the family expects an engagement soon. Elinor wonders what she will do without her sister. “We will miss her dearly. But she will be happy,” her mother says.

Later, Margaret watches Willoughby and Marianne talk in the distance. Sir John arrives with a letter from Edward to Elinor’s happiness. Mrs. Dashwood gushes with Margaret thinking a double wedding is in the family’s future. Elinor then tells them Edward wrote that he is not coming, that business in London has impeded his visit. Mrs. Dashwood can tell her daughter is crushed, but Elinor composes herself for Marianne’s sake, saying it is a happy day, expecting Marianne to get an offer of marriage.

However, that is not meant to be. Marianne returns to the cottage shell shocked. Willoughby has told her that he has to go back to London and won’t be able to return for a year. She wonders if a love can last that kind of distance and time. Mrs. Dashwood comforts her.

Elinor, meanwhile, suffers her pain in silence.

Invited to another dinner party with Sir John, a depressed Marianne is less than enthused to attend. However, when she hears that one of Mrs. Jennings daughters, Mrs. Palmer is attending, who lives in London, Marianne pulls herself together, formulating a plan. At the party meeting Mrs. Palmer (Bethany Slater) a loud, talkative woman like her mother and her dour, quiet husband Mr. Palmer (Eliot Sumner), Marianne convinces Mrs. Jennings to let Elinor and her chaperone her back to London so they can visit. Meanwhile, Elinor meets Lucy Steele (Ceara Coveney) and asks about Edward. Lucy tells Elinor he is well and that he said Elinor made his time “perfectly tolerable” implying Edward has a strictly platonic feeling for her.

The next day, as they prep the carriages to go to London, Marianne is met by Brandon, who tells him of her journey to London, hoping to meet Willoughby. Brandon asks of his intentions towards her, hinting that he knows more about the man’s past. Marianne says her intentions and Willoughby’s intentions are the same. Brandon, hurt, but composed, tells Marianne that he wishes her great happiness and that Willoughby will do right by her to deserve her. He rides off.

Elinor, Marianne, and Mrs. Jennings travel to London. Over the journey, Marianne lets it slip that she wrote to Willoughby where she is staying so he could come visit.

At Mrs. Jennings house, Elinor gets a letter for Edward.

On a group outing later, Elinor walks with Lucy who tells her in confidence that she and Edward have been engaged for years, though his family does not approve. To twist the knife further, Lucy says Edward sees Elinor “like a sister.”

Marianne writes to Willoughby but has yet to get a response from her multiple letters.

Soon after, Edward arrives to have a private audience with Elinor. He tells Elinor that he has come to apologize, that his previous conduct with her was unbecoming a gentleman and he must confess that he has been engaged for many years to Lucy Steele. Having the rumor confirmed breaks something in Elinor; she cannot believe it.

Elinor asks if he came here to humiliate her. Edwards says no, and claims he did not know he was engaged. When Elinor scoffs, Edward explains the match was made when they were children for the betterment of the two families. However, when Lucy’s family lost her fortune, his family urged him to break the engagement. Having not heard from Lucy in years, he had hoped she had found another to marry but she has not, and he feels he must keep his promise, even as his family threatens to disinherit him. Elinor is taken aback by his honor. “Your honor is worth more than your family?” she says, astounded. “You cannot love her,” Elinor says, her true feeling slipping out, but Edward says he will do what is right and takes his leave.

Marianne comes to comfort Elinor, though Elinor claims that they parted as friends. Marianne then says they have nothing to talk about seeing as she conceals nothing while Elinor hides everything, hoping her sister will just be honest for once about what she feels.

Later that evening, Mrs. Jennings speaks about a Winter Ball, where she knows Willoughby and Edward will most likely be attending, knowing the affection the two Dashwood sisters have for them.

At the party, Marianne searches for Willoughby. Elinor sees Lucy and has to deal with her gushing over Edward’s arrival. Elinor also crosses paths with John Dashwood and Fanny, and meets Fanny’s younger brother Robert Ferrars. Robert immediately sees Lucy and asks about her, only for Fanny to tell him to look elsewhere, as the family has tried to get rid of her for years. Yet, Robert, entranced by her surface beauty, cannot look away.

Marianne continues to search for Willoughby.

Using the excuse of looking for Marianne, Elinor excuses herself. Going up the stairs, she crosses paths with Edward. Edward asks for her to dance with him and she accepts. They dance, their eyes locked to one another. Nothing else in the world exists. Fanny looks at Elinor with rage, wanting her to have nothing to do with her brother. Her husband smiles, in defiance of his wife’s cruelty, and perhaps wanting the two to be happy. However, Lucy also sees them dance and becomes angry, which Edward sees and quickly excuses himself.

Marianne finally locates Willoughby but he is cold, stiff, and distant. When Marianne presses him, asking why he didn’t respond to her letters, he reveals that he is newly engaged to Lady Jane Grey. Marianne tells him he doesn’t understand.

Elinor sees Mrs. Jennings and Mrs. Jennings says she was trying to find her, having found out Willoughby is engaged to another woman, which she cannot believe, as she had been telling everyone he was engaged to Marianne. Elinor finds Marianne. Marianne makes a fool of herself screaming his name. Elinor pulls Marianne away and they leave the party. Brandon, who was in attendance as well, witnesses her devastation. Mrs. Jennings curses Willoughby for his cruelty.

Back at Mrs. Jennings, Marianne is distraught and cannot understand why Willoughby was so cold to her. Elinor doesn’t understand it either, believing they had an engagement. Marianne then confesses despite his gifts and attention they had no formal engagement agreement but it still does not explain his utter indifference. When Elinor asks why Marianne didn’t confide in her any of this, Marianne says, “Because you are always right! And I always resent it.”

Elinor receives a letter from Colonel Brandon telling her that he had information about Willoughby’s character, but held back to spare Marianne’s feelings. However, he has given Elinor what he knows and leaves it up to her judgment whether or not to tell Marianne. Elinor ultimately tells Marianne that Willoughby seduced a widow only to abandon her when she was pregnant, and who ultimately died in childbirth.

The next morning, Fanny, John, and Robert meet with Elinor and Marianne. They relate that because Edward refused to break his engagement with Lucy, the family disinherited him. Marianne calls Lucy out for being selfish and opportunistic and Fanny actually agrees with her. Elinor points out that Robert is now the heir to the family fortune, to which he sheepishly agrees.

Marianne talks privately with Elinor, noting that Lucy will not marry Edward, since he no longer has his fortune. Elinor tells her that Colonel Brandon, having heard of his situation and greatly impressed with his moral integrity, has offered him a church position where he lives, allowing him a profession so he can marry Lucy.

Marianne balks at the news. “But Edward loves you!”

Elinor counters her sister that Edward is doing the right thing and when Marianne presses her on her feelings, Elinor finally snaps. “You think true passion can never be checked!” Elinor tells Marianne that Edward is a good and noble man, her perfect match, but he is doing what he must, and so must she, noting that sometimes love is not enough. “Can you ever think of me capable of feeling?” Elinor asks her sister, trying to convey how torn up she is about Edward marrying Lucy. Marianne apologizes and hugs her sister.

Edward meets Elinor at an art gallery. He is amazed Brandon offered him a job. Elinor tells Edward he must do what is right and marry Lucy, that he is a man of his word. Edward, obviously ambivalent about marrying a woman he barely knows nor loves, says he could break the engagement, but Elinor tells him to do no such thing. If he were to do so, he would hate himself, and she would not think highly of him anymore. They sit in silence for a moment.

“So we will marry,” Edward says with great reluctance, obviously wishing he could say it to her. Elinor looks at him and wishes him the greatest happiness possible. Edward tells her she has been his dearest friend, which she affirms as well. Overcome with emotion, Elinor leaves.

Their trip to London ending in failure, Marianne and Elinor travel back to Barton with Mrs. Jennings; Colonel Brandon is with them as an escort.

Halfway there, they stop at the home of Mr. Palmer who allows them to rest. Marianne goes out for a walk, though warned by Mrs. Jennings to not go far as to walk near the estate of Willoughby. Marianne is surprised he lives nearby, and Mr. Palmer lets it be known he despises the man.

Marianne walks and it begins to rain. Despite the warning, Marianne travels to Willoughby estate and screams his name in anguish, breaking down sobbing. She tries to find her way back but becomes delirious and sick.

Marianne returns to the Palmer home and is placed by the fire by Mrs. Jennings. Elinor believes her to be overreacting and does not take her state of mind seriously.

That night, Brandon comes to sit by the fire with her. Brandon tells her his story and how Willoughby is tied into it. Years before, he was in love with a woman named Eliza who was a ward of his father. Though they loved each other, she was to be married to his older brother when Eliza turned twenty. Brandon and Eliza attempted to elope, but it failed and they were discovered. She was married off to his brother and he was sent into his military life (implying he was exiled into a career he did not want). He returned years later after his brother died, to find Eliza suffered greatly in an unhappy marriage. Brandon spent months searching for her only to find her pregnant and abandoned. Eliza ran towards the first man who had treated her well in years, who was Willoughby. However, once he learned that Eliza would not inherit her husband’s estate (Brandon would), Willoughby left her. Marianne asks where Eliza is; Brandon tells both Eliza and the child died.

Days later, Marianne’s health has declined. A doctor is sent for, and he is unsure if she will live or not. When the doctor hears Mrs. Dashwood is not present, he urges her to be summoned, as he cannot guarantee she will have a chance to say goodbye. Brandon offers to travel to retrieve Mrs. Dashwood. “I will be of use!” Brandon says.

Mrs. Jennings and Elinor tend to Marianne. Elinor lies next to her sister and cries. “You cannot leave me, Marianne.”

Days later, in the early morning, Elinor hears a knock at the door. She runs towards it, thinking it is her mother. Instead, it is a drunken Willoughby asking breathlessly if Marianne is okay. As he paces the room, Elinor tells him he is in no condition to see her. Willoughby notes that yes, he is drunk, but he came over because he loves Marianne. While initially sympathetic, Elinor’s capacity withers when she remembers Willoughby is newly married and how he treated her sister. When she calls out his behavior, Willoughby tries to defend it, saying he was just having fun with Marianne but came to genuinely care for her and planned to propose but his aunt called him home to answer for “rumors” of his past actions.

Elinor realizes he is talking about Eliza and is disgusted. Willoughby once again tries to defend himself, claiming he didn’t know about the child and that Eliza was a “worldly woman” and thought she would just return home. By this point, Elinor’s sympathy for him is all but gone. It is eroded to nothing when Colonel Brandon and her mother arrive. Elinor tells them Marianne has recovered and that Willoughby is about to leave. When Willoughby objects and angrily says Elinor has never been so uncivil, Elinor loses her cool and tells him she has no idea what she is capable of. Brandon then tells him to leave. Willoughby scoffs and says Brandon forgets himself, as he has no right to make him leave as it is not his house. Having had enough of the man, who has now hurt two women he loved, Brandon grabs Willoughby and forcefully ejects him from the house.

Mrs. Jennings, Mrs. Dashwood, Elinor, and Marianne watch stunned from the bedroom window as Brandon challenges Willoughby to a duel. At ten paces, the two men turn to face each other and fire. Brandon shoots his pistol in the air. Willoughby fires at Brandon but outright misses. Marianne asks about Brandon to the shock of her family. “I knew Brandon had great passion,” she says. For in that moment, she sees both men differently. Brandon, as trained soldier, had the means and skill to kill Willoughby, a man that had greatly wronged him and the women he loved. Yet, Brandon resisted doing so, and only made the duel occur to show Willoughby that his actions can have consequences. Willoughby, by firing at Brandon, has shown himself an immature child that only takes what he wants and expects others to pay for his mistakes.

Having revealed his true character, Willoughby drops his pistol and runs back to his estate, having lost Marianne forever, and will live in a loveless marriage, haunted by the shame of his actions.

As Brandon returns to the house, they place Marianne back into bed. Marianne asks if he is okay. Brandon says Willoughby is okay. “She was asking about you,” Mrs. Jennings says. Brandon tells her he is unharmed; Marianne smiles.

When Marianne fully recovers, the family returns to the cottage in Barton with Colonel Brandon. Margaret is overjoyed to see her sisters again and asks about London. They both tell her it wasn’t that great. “Places are like people. They’re never what you expect,” Marianne tells her.

Brandon and Marianne go riding on their horses, growing closer. Marianne tells Brandon that her illness has made her different. Brandon says he hopes not, because she is great the way she is. Marianne clarifies that she once believed she would never love again, though her near death experience has made her happy to see that is not true. Choosing his words carefully, Brandon asks if she believes, in time, she could love another. Marianne says she could, perhaps even greater than before. Brandon quietly nods, understanding what she is trying to tell him. They could have a future together, but she needs time to heal her heartbreak, and Brandon is willing to give her that time to do so.

The family learns of Edward’s apparent marriage to Lucy. Elinor is distraught and her family tries to comfort her. Margaret looks outside and to her surprise says Edward is arriving. Mrs. Dashwood offers to send him away, but Elinor tells her family she will face him, and asks to be left alone. Wiping tears from her eyes, she tries to pull it together. “I WILL BE MISTRESS OF MYSELF,” Elinor intones.

Edward enters the cottage and the reunion is awkward from the start. Believing him to be married, Elinor is hostile with him, wondering why he has come to see her. As Edward seemingly is ready to declare his love, Elinor, believing him acting dishonorably as a married man, rejects him and sends him away. Edward apologizes and walks away.

As Elinor tends to the laundry, her mother commends her for being strong. Mrs. Jennings arrives, having seen Edward on the way there, looking sad. She notes of the recent gossip in London that Lucy has married, but not to Edward, but to Robert, the new heir. Mrs. Dashwood speaks harshly of Lucy for abandoning Edward after all he did to protect her, while Mrs. Jennings counters it was almost a foregone conclusion given she had no money or skills. Elinor, shocked, asks if what Mrs. Jennings said was true, realizing she made a terrible mistake. The family realizes the same, and tells her to run after him.

Elinor chases after Edward and finally finds him on the path. She calls out to him and asks him if he is truly not married. Edward tells her he is not. Edward came back for her because she and Colonel Brandon gave him his freedom; when he was disinherited, Brandon gave him a job at the church, but Lucy didn’t want that life and left him. Edwards says he has loved Elinor from the moment he saw her and though the life he will have now is neither much nor what she deserves he had hoped it was not too late. Elinor responds by kissing him passionately. “It is as much as I ever wanted,” Elinor tells him, smiling.

The happy couple returns to the cottage, engaged. Mrs. Dashwood, Mrs. Jennings, Marianne, and Margaret are overjoyed for the two. As the group go inside to celebrate the impending wedding, Elinor and Marianne share a private, sisterly hug. Their path to happiness is on the horizon and they will get to share in it, together.

wiki_plot.text:
The Dashwood sisters – Elinor, Marianne and Margaret – and their mother face potential poverty when Mr Dashwood's estate passes to their half-brother John and his snobbish wife, Fanny. Fanny persuades John to withhold the inheritance his father had suggested he provide, and the couple move into the estate, disrupting the sisters' lives. Fanny's brother, Edward Ferrars, visits and forms a close bond with Elinor, much to Fanny's dismay. Mrs Jennings, a distant relative of the Dashwoods, offers them a Devonshire cottage owned by her son-in-law, Sir John Middleton, at a reduced rent. Mrs Dashwood accepts, while Elinor hopes Edward will propose, although he merely promises to visit.

In Devonshire, Marianne initially finds Colonel Brandon, a family friend of Mrs Jennings, unappealing, despite her interest in hearing about him. Brandon, however, develops feelings for Marianne. Elinor becomes saddened when Edward writes to say he will not visit. Meanwhile, Marianne sprains her ankle while visiting the beach with Margaret and is rescued by John Willoughby, to whom she is immediately attracted. They begin courting, but just as the family anticipate a proposal, Willoughby abruptly announces that he must travel to London and will be gone for 12 months.

Mrs Jennings invites Elinor and Marianne to London with Lady Middleton and her cousin Lucy Steele, where they expect Edward to visit. Lucy, aware of Elinor's feelings for Edward, reveals that she and Edward have been secretly engaged for years. Edward explains that his parents arranged the match in the expectation of Lucy's wealth, but he refused to abandon her after she lost her fortune. Having hoped Lucy would end the engagement herself, he nevertheless remains bound by honour. Heartbroken, Elinor accepts the situation and promises to keep their secret.

Willoughby ignores Marianne's letters and fails to visit the Dashwoods in London. Hoping to see him at a ball, Marianne is devastated when he arrives with his wealthy fiancée, Miss Grey, and treats her coldly. Overcome with anguish, she makes a spectacle of herself before admitting to Elinor that she and Willoughby were never formally engaged. She insists that, unlike Elinor, she cannot quietly accept her disappointment. Colonel Brandon subsequently reveals that Willoughby seduced and impregnated his widowed sister-in-law, Eliza, before abandoning her; she later died with her unborn child.

When the Ferrars family discovers Edward's engagement, he is disinherited and his younger brother Robert becomes the heir. Impressed by Edward's integrity, Brandon offers him a nearby parsonage, enabling him to marry. During what she believes will be her final conversation with Edward, Elinor urges him to honour his commitment.

On their return journey, Mrs Jennings takes the Dashwood sisters and Brandon to visit her youngest daughter. Learning that Willoughby's estate is nearby, Marianne walks out in the rain to see it and consequently becomes gravely ill. Willoughby subsequently arrives unexpectedly, drunk, and professes his love for Marianne, pleading to see her. Elinor's sympathy diminishes when he dismisses his treatment of Eliza, and Brandon forcibly ejects him after returning to collect Mrs Dashwood. The family watch from Marianne's room as Brandon has challenged Willoughby to a duel. Neither is injured: Willoughby misses, while Brandon deliberately fires into the air. Unexpectedly, Marianne expresses concern only for Brandon's safety.

Marianne recovers, and the party returns to Devonshire. She grows closer to Brandon, suggesting they might have a future together once she has recovered from her heartbreak. He willingly gives her time. The family subsequently learns that Lucy has become Mrs Ferrars, and Edward arrives, apparently intending to declare his love for Elinor. Believing he has behaved dishonourably, Elinor rejects him and sends him away. Mrs Jennings later reveals that Lucy abandoned Edward after his disinheritance and married Robert instead, to secure a wealthy husband. Overjoyed, Elinor rushes to Edward, declares her love and becomes engaged to him.

spoiler_text.text:
The film opens in Mossy Bottom Farm. Shaun, Timmy (both Justin Fletcher), Bitzer, The Farmer (both John Sparkes), and the rest of the flock wake up and get ready to do their chores. The sheep are growing pumpkins in time for Halloween, keeping them hidden for protection.

The farm is visited by a Vet (Nina Sosanya), whom The Farmer is smitten with. Bitzer and the sheep hide from her to avoid getting their medicine, but she is able to quickly find them (except Bitzer) and administer the medicine into their mouths. The Vet also appears to return The Farmer’s feelings. She plans to invite him to a Halloween event (one that he was already planning to invite her to), but The Farmer gets yanked away by his goat. He ends up crashing into the flock’s pumpkin patch, destroying all the gourds, to the dismay of the sheep.

Shaun finds a science book and comes up with an idea to produce large pumpkins quickly to replace the ones that were ruined. He creates a potion like a mad scientist and adds it to the seeds after planting them. Since Shaun put it inside an empty container of hair growth formula, Bitzer returns it to The Farmer, who was hoping to regrow his hair to impress The Vet. He adds some to his head before going to bed.

In the morning, The Farmer has grown more hair on his head, and then on his face. The flock’s pumpkins have also grown rapidly. The Farmer puts on an ill-fitting leather outfit to meet The Vet and invite her to the Halloween event. However, Shaun sees that the pumpkins are STILL growing.

At The Vet’s office, The Farmer sees that the hair on his face, head, and body are growing even larger. He is forced to hide from The Vet, and The Farmer’s entire body becomes covered in hair. He accidentally steps in cement, and the stuff that hardens on his feet make his footsteps loud and thunderous. The Farmer returns to Mossy Bottom and frightens the other animals.

Shaun and the flock hide in the bathroom, while Bitzer hides elsewhere. The Farmer enters the bathroom to try and shave himself. Shaun sees his glasses and quickly realizes who it is, alerting the other sheep but keeping it from Bitzer.

The sheep go to a cave where they find The Farmer having failed to remove his hair, because it just grows back right away. When he rips it off, he lets out a loud yell that is heard in Mossingham, frightening the townsfolk. After The Farmer leaves and ends up in town, he is exposed after posing as a statue, and everyone freaks out. The Shopkeeper (Paul Whitehouse) leads the mob against The Farmer. Meanwhile, The Vet sees The Farmer’s big footprint and begins to believe that Bigfoot is in town, and she hopes to send the “beast” to an island with other sasquatches. When Bitzer finds the cave and sees The Farmer’s glasses, he assumes his master was eaten, until Shaun eventually tells him the truth.

The Farmer gets incapacitated, and The Vet manages to get him on a boat. Shaun leads the flock to the dock and distract the crew so that they can get the crate that The Farmer is stashed in. Bitzer tries to get into the control seat, but he gets stuck in a stink gas that the sheep threw in, and he gets the boat moving. The sheep get the crate off the boat before it sails, but when they open it, it’s full of fuzzy dolls, and The Farmer is still on the boat. The sheep leave, defeated.

When they get back to the farm, the flock sees that the pumpkins have grown to such a colossal size that they have destroyed parts of the farm. Shaun is shut out by the other sheep. He goes back to the cave, where the others meet him later. They find The Farmer’s phone and see numerous missed calls from The Vet. Shaun remembers that they shared a connection, so he gets an idea. He draws a picture on the cave wall to try and explain to The Vet that the “beast” is really The Farmer. She gets it and hops on a boat to go after him, with Shaun sneaking onboard. The Vet helps other stuck animals in the ocean, who end up helping her and Shaun catch up to the ship. The Vet is able to free The Farmer, and everyone sails back to land.

Shaun returns to the barn and gathers the flock to create an antidote for The Farmer. The townspeople spot The Farmer and chase him to the windmill where Shaun is setting up the antidote, and The Shopkeeper even tries to prevent The Vet from helping. The Farmer gets stuck on the windmill until Timmy and the other sheep arrive with a giant pumpkin and make it look like it eats The Farmer. Shaun gets the antidote ready and sprays it on The Farmer, removing all his hair and turning him back to normal. The Vet then pushes the giant pumpkin to scare away the townsfolk, and it grabs The Shopkeeper in its mouth.

Later on, The Farmer and The Vet get together to go to the Halloween event. Shaun, Bitzer, and the flock fashion the pumpkins into giant Jack-o-lanterns, and then they have a party in the barn.

During the credits, a crow is seen drinking what’s left of the growth formula, and it starts to glow ominously…

wiki_plot.text:
During the lead-up to Halloween on the Mossy Bottom farm, the farmer accidentally destroys his sheep flock's secret pumpkin patch. Shaun discovers a book on home-made science and becomes a mad scientist to fix the problem. He creates a potion to regrow the pumpkins instantly, but the container is misplaced and Shaun mistakenly mixes the potion with the farmer's bottle of hair-growth serum. After Shaun plants the first seed, the farmer's dog Bitzer obliviously returns the bottle. The farmer applies it to his head, hoping to impress the town vet, with whom he has a mutual crush. The mixed potion causes the farmer's hair to grow wildly out of control, turning him into a shaggy beast resembling Bigfoot. The farm animals are frightened by the farmer's appearance, mistaking him for a beast. While hiding from him in his house, the sheep realise the beast is the farmer. The farmer fails to stop the hair from growing and retreats to a cave. Bitzer tracks him down, unaware of his transformation. The farmer goes after Bitzer, who flees in terror thinking the beast ate the farmer; he tries to escape in the farmer's pickup truck which the farmer and the sheep end up on. Bitzer loses the farmer upon reaching the town, where Shaun explains the situation to him.

While stumbling through the Mossingham town, the farmer inadvertently scares the townspeople. The vet aspires to capture the beast with the hope of sending him to Bigfoot Island, also unaware it is the farmer. Despite extreme backlash from the townspeople, she tranquillises the farmer and has him shipped to Bigfoot Island. Bitzer and the sheep steal a crate from a ship presumably carrying the farmer, but they find it is full of stuffed toys and the farmer is still to the island.

The farm animals return home dismayed and Shaun gives up his mad scientist persona, feeling guilty for his actions. Upon finding several missed calls from the vet on the farmer's phone, Shaun enlists her help. Through DNA testing, she discovers the farmer is the beast. Shaun and the vet chase after the ship on a motorboat and rescue the farmer. He and the flock race to make an antidote for the growth potion as the farm's pumpkins begin to grow uncontrollably. Back at the farm, the locals rally against the "beast" and chase him to the windmill where Shaun created the potion. Using an overgrown carved pumpkin and a tractor, Bitzer and Timmy create the illusion that the beast has been eaten. Shaun sprays the antidote into the mouth of the carved pumpkin, returning the farmer to normal. The farmer and the vet invite each other to a local Halloween dance party, while the flock holds a secret Halloween party of their own. Meanwhile, a crow drinks the remnants of the growth potion out of a bin.

spoiler_text.text:
The film opens as shepherd George Hardy (Hugh Jackman) is writing a letter to someone named Rebecca. He tells her all about the sheep in his meadow, and how all of them are special, but he has a few that he spends a lot of time with. There are ram brothers Reggie and Ronnie (both Brett Goldstein), who love to bash things; Zora (Bella Ramsey), a curious little lamb; Cloud (Regina Hall), a sheep who is a bit of a “diva”; Sir Richfield (Patrick Stewart), a sophisticated sheep, Wool-Eyes (Rhys Darby), a sheep who cannot see because of the wool over his eyes; and Mopple (Chris O’Dowd), a ram that has an excellent memory. For George, the two sheep that are most special to him are Sebastian (Bryan Cranston), a black ram who wanders from the meadow every now and then; and Lily (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), who always listens to George’s crime stories.

George frequently goes into the nearby town of Denbrook, where he tells Rebecca about some of the locals. There is another shepherd named Caleb Merrow (Tosin Cole), whom George is not fond of; Ham Gilyard (Conleth Hill), a butcher that George REALLY doesn’t like; Beth Pennock (Hong Chau), an innkeeper that has a grudge against George; Tim Derry (Nicholas Braun), a bumbling police officer; and Reverend Hillcoate (Kobna Holbrook-Smith), a preacher that also has some issue with George. George walks into the congregation during Hillcoate’s sermon and puts a big wad of cash in the offering before leaving.

On the meadow, the flock is rude to a small unnamed Winter Lamb (Tommy Birchall) since he is small and not the same as those born in the spring. George picks the lamb up and feeds it, as he thinks they all deserve to be treated equally. Caleb arrives to speak with George for a moment, but he is promptly sent leaving after a few minutes. Whenever the sheep want to forget something unpleasant, they all collectively choose to forget, but Mopple cannot forget even if he tried.

At the inn, Beth finds from the postwoman that George is writing to Rebecca using rose-scented paper. Beth swipes the letter from the bag. Moments later, she is visited by a reporter named Elliot Matthews (Nicholas Galitzine), who is covering the cultural festival of Denbrook. Beth takes him around to show him it’s just three lousy stands with barely any “culture” to display. As Elliot is later getting home, he crashes his car into a tree in the rain. Meanwhile at George’s home, there is a knock on his door that startles him awake.

In the morning, Lily and Mopple go to discover George’s body lying in the grass. Mopple has to explain to Lily that George is dead and that he has not “become a cloud” like how she believes sheep end up when they pass on. Lily is heartbroken and breaks the news to the rest of the flock that their shepherd is gone. Tim comes upon the body and believes it to be a heart attack at first, until he investigates the inside of George’s trailer and sees that he shared a drink with someone and believes that he was poisoned. Elliot, who looked in the trailer with Tim, thinks he’s got a murder case he can report on.

Lily tells the flock what she overheard and thinks this is a mystery that they need to solve. Sebastian returns and thinks they are dumb for attempting to solve something when they are just animals, but he is convinced to join Lily and Mopple as they travel into Denbrook. First, Lily and Mopple have to get over their fear of crossing the road since it’s the first time they are seeing something not covered in grass.

The townsfolk gather for a reading of George’s will from his lawyer, Lydia Harbottle (Emma Thompson), one altered from his previous will. Also arriving is Rebecca Hampstead (Molly Gordon), who is revealed to be George’s daughter from the United States (and Tim is quickly smitten with her). Elliot shows up to the reading but is forced by Lydia to stay out of the room. Lydia reads the will in the presence of Tim, Rebecca, Caleb, Ham, Beth, and Hillcoate, as well as calling a man named Peter Van Vuuren, who turns out to be George’s son/Rebecca’s twin who was given up for adoption in South Africa. The will also calls out the attendees as “two murderers, a victim, a fool, a winter lamb, and a bad shepherd”. Most notably is that George has left both halves of his acres to his children, including $30 million for Rebecca since George patented a blue medicine for sheep to help with a condition called orf. The motive is now made known. Outside, Mopple gets into a mess when he runs blindly through the building after getting a grass-stained sheet on his face. Caleb leads him out safely.

Back on the meadow, the sheep try to solve the murder themselves. The Winter Lamb mentions seeing George’s “ghost” leaving his body in the night, but the others dismiss this claim. The sheep also spot Rebecca walking along the meadow, despite having earlier told Tim she has never visited her father’s meadow. Sebastian also objects to the flock’s treatment of the Winter Lamb, since he was born outside the spring as well. He tells Lily about his backstory, where he aged out of the petting zoo at the carnival and was forced to fight with dogs until George rescued him.

Tim begins his investigation by narrowing down the suspects from the will reading and their motives against George, and is joined by Elliot so he can get a good story. He finds out that Beth swiped George’s letter to Rebecca, as well as how he and Ham had issues because George was a vegetarian (not exactly a butcher’s friend). Caleb had his lease on the meadow canceled by George. As for why George dropped the cash into Hillcoate’s plate during his sermon, Hillcoate admits that he and George were involved in some business that led to a falling out, which is why he knows that the will was addressing him, not Caleb, as the “bad shepherd”. Tim and Elliot also confront Rebecca after finding out her real name is “Chastity Cramps” and that she had indeed been at the meadow before.

The sheep learn from Cloud that Rebecca had been by the meadow before the previous night, as she had dropped a bracelet on the ground. Due to their continued distrust of the Winter Lamb, Sebastian ends up leaving the flock again.

Lily finds Tim and leads him back to the meadow so he can find Rebecca’s bracelet. He arrives at her location with Elliot and Beth to arrest her on suspicion of George’s murder. Adding to this is that Tim finds the poison berry used to kill George stuck to the bottom of her shoe. Rebecca protests that she is innocent and how she had been communicating with George via letters since he had always felt guilty about having to give her up for adoption since he was very young.

Knowing that their flock will merge with Caleb’s flock soon, Lily and Mopple cross into his meadow to meet the rest of the sheep. One of them simply approaches Lily and ominously warns her to run. She and Mopple then come across a picture of Caleb and Ham shaking hands, as they realize that this farm is meant to slaughter the sheep for meat (thus making them the “two murderers”). Two German shepherd guard dogs chase Lily and Mopple into the meadow, but they are defended by Sebastian. Unfortunately, he is fatally wounded by a dog bite, and he dies next to Lily. This forces her to come to terms with the fact that sheep die just like humans and do not become clouds, something that Mopple has to break to her since she has willfully forgotten the same thing happened to other sheep like her parents. Lily says the grief is too hard for her to remember, but Mopple tells her it’s necessary for her to hold on to the memories of her loved ones like George.

Lily and Mopple return to the flock, breaking the news about Sebastian to them. As she prepares to give up, Lily sees a vision of George speaking to her and understanding her. This gives her the encouragement she needs to bring his killer to justice.

Lily gets back on the case and joins Mopple as they recruit the Winter Lamb to go into George’s trailer and find something that can help them. They then go back to the station at Denbrook where Rebecca is being held, and the Winter Lamb sneaks in to paint a message on the floor. In the morning, Tim sees a blue line and a yellow line connected to a picture of George, ending in a smudge of green mixed together.

The people gather in the middle of town as Rebecca is being transferred for prosecution. However, Tim sees Lily, Mopple, and the Winter Lamb with his hooves covered in paint. The pieces come together for Tim, and he stops to reveal to everyone he knows who the real killer is (Rebecca is “the victim”). The real killer was someone who was not physically at the will reading: Mr. Peter Van Vuuren, AKA…ELLIOT MATTHEWS. Since George was found with one hand covered in blue and the other in green, Tim knew that the blue was from his sheep medicine, and the green was from Peter’s hair dye mixed with the medicine in a struggle as he had poisoned George after visiting him following his “car accident”. It was easy for him to elude suspicion since Lydia kicked him out of the room, allowing him to call without being detected. He had hoped to acquire George’s $30 million inheritance if Rebecca were convicted, going as far as to plant the poison berry on her shoe. Peter nearly weasels his way out until Tim pulls a hair off him that could be analyzed and convict him. Peter attempts to escape, but Reggie and Ronnie are called for “a legitimate cause for bashing”. They destroy Peter’s car and leave him to be arrested.

In the aftermath, Lydia tells Rebecca that the new will cannot be honored, so the original will stipulates she will inherit George’s land. When Caleb and Ham try to get Rebecca to sell the land to them, she refuses and instead buys Caleb’s sheep from him, growing the flock even more as she stays on the land. Before Rebecca returns to the meadow, a repentant Beth gives her the last letter George wrote to her. The rose-scented paper gave her the impression that George was writing to a lover, which makes Rebecca realize Beth was in love with him (making her the “winter lamb”, or a “reject”). She admits that although they did try for a romance, George’s heart always belonged to Rebecca’s mother, who was named Lily.

Rebecca returns to the meadow with Caleb’s sheep and sits to read the flock a book written by George. Lily goes to find the Winter Lamb and welcome him to the flock, even naming him after George. As Lily returns with George to the flock, she looks up to the sky and sees a cloud that looks like Sebastian.

wiki_plot.text:
On his farm near the English village of Denbrook, shepherd George Hardy spends his time looking after his flock of sheep and reading murder mystery novels to them. The sheep live in blissful ignorance, believing that death only exists in fiction and that they turn into clouds at the end of their lives. When faced with an uncomfortable situation, they can will themselves to forget. They discriminate against an orphan lamb born in winter rather than the typical spring.

One morning, George is discovered dead outside his trailer. Reporter Elliot Matthews believes he was murdered and encourages Officer Tim Derry to investigate. Tim concludes that George was poisoned. The sheep decide to solve the mystery on their own, led by crime aficionado ewe Lily, the ram Mopple who always keeps his memories, and stoic loner Sebastian whom George rescued from a carnival.

During the reading of George's will—attended by Elliot, Tim, George's solicitor Lydia Harbottle, Reverend Hillcoate, butcher Ham Gilyard, innkeeper Beth Pennock, and neighbouring shepherd Caleb Merrow—they learn that George had a twin son and daughter who were sent away for adoption after their mother died in childbirth. The daughter, Rebecca Hampstead, also in attendance, reconnected with George and had just arrived from the United States to visit him for the first time. Lydia ousts Elliot before calling George's son, Peter Van Vuuren, who lives in South Africa, so he can attend remotely. They learn George was secretly a millionaire after selling the patent for an orf medicine he invented. The new will awards his fortune to Rebecca, replacing an old will which donated it to an animal rights charity.

Cloud, a member of the flock, reveals she found one of Rebecca's bangles the night of the murder, contradicting Rebecca's claim of never having met her father. The sheep lead Tim to the meadow where he finds the bangle. He then discovers the type of berry used to poison George squashed in the soles of Rebecca's boots, and she is placed under arrest. 

Lily and Mopple, soon to be taken in by Caleb, visit his meadow to meet their future flock mates, but discover that Caleb owns a slaughterhouse and has been collaborating with Ham to slaughter sheep for meat. They are attacked and chased by Caleb's vicious German Shepherds, but Sebastian returns and fights the dogs in order to protect Lily and Mopple. Despite suffering grievous wounds during the fight, Sebastian manages to drive the dogs off before dying from his injuries. Lily realises that death is real, and that she had willed herself to forget every time a sheep close to her died.

Lily tries to lead the other sheep to safety, but they become terrified and will themselves to forget, leaving her despondent. Mopple encourages her to embrace her memories of their deceased loved ones. Lily still tries to forget George but speaks to his ghost and realises that Rebecca is innocent and has been framed by the real killer. She and Mopple recruit the winter lamb to sneak into the jail and paint a message with his hooves.

Tim is in the process of handing Rebecca over to the county police officers when he suddenly suspects that she is innocent. The sheep help Tim conclude that "Elliot" is Peter. Peter dyed his hair and assumed a new identity before murdering George, whose hands were stained in the scuffle by the medicine and dye. Peter then forged a will to make it appear that Rebecca had a motive, so after her conviction he would inherit his father's fortune as his next-of-kin. Peter attempts to flee, but twin rams Ronnie and Reggie destroy his car. Peter is arrested by the county police while Rebecca is cleared of all charges.

Rebecca learns from Beth that her and Peter's mother was named Lily. Rebecca takes her father's surname, claims ownership of the meadow and sheep, and buys Caleb's French-speaking sheep to keep Caleb and Ham from slaughtering them. As Rebecca sits down to read to the flock, Lily adopts the Winter Lamb, naming him George. She looks towards the sunset and sees a cloud resembling Sebastian.

spoiler_text.text:
Prologue: White Girl Wasted
The film starts as a woman named Kayleigh (Portia Doubleday) standing outside her overheated car. Two deputies, Otumbo and Diaz (Michael Braugher and Sierra Capri), approach Kayleigh, who says she called for a tow truck. She is clearly drunk and grows belligerent, eventually taking out her phone to record her being “harassed” before she starts spewing racial vitriol against both cops. When Kayleigh explicitly threatens to kill Diaz, the two place her under arrest.

In her apartment, data scientist Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) watches Kayleigh’s video on Facebook, which is being shared on an alt-right extremist group called Voices of Reason.

Part One: Cassandra
2019 – At the Wall Street Journal in San Francisco, Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) meets with his new employers Christina (Betty Gilpin), Tom (Nelson Franklin), and Andy (Gbenga Akinnagbe). He is tasked with covering Facebook. Jeff mainly writes in politics and is not even on Facebook, though he immediately signs up at his bosses’ urging.

Frances, who works with the Civic Integrity Team at Facebook, attends a meeting held by media relations executive Teddy Marks (Billy Magnussen). Teddy tells everyone about how “Facebook detectives” like Jeff are trying to contact Facebook employees to try and dig information out of them. When Frances tries to bring up her concerns about the Kayleigh video and other findings on the app, Teddy ends the meeting early. Her other colleagues do not care to hear her out either and instead suggest she uses a new dating app. Frances ends up going on a date with an idiot finance bro who gets false medical information (drinking chlorophyll as a substitute for deodorant) from Facebook.

Jeff works with two interns, Zach and Evelyn (Aidan Laprete and Kelley Pereira), to try and get in touch with someone at Facebook, but pretty much everyone has told him to fuck off. Jeff finally ends up messaging Frances, who sets up a private meeting with him in the park. She shows him the Kayleigh video and brings him her research of how the site is radicalizing far-right extremists by targeting up to 64% of users, and that Kayleigh, who used to be friends with Frances, is one of them. Frances wants to keep her identity as anonymous as possible and asks Jeff to find out about MSI (Meaningful Social Interactions).

A brief jump to January 2021 shows Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) being coached by a crisis management specialist named Raya (Wunmi Mosaku) ahead of his testimony before the U.S. Senate. The group has brought in reporter and former Facebook investor Charlie Garrigan (Bill Burr) to come in and be as blunt as possible with Mark. Charlie also asks Mark what MSI stands for.

Part Two: Meaningful Social Interactions
Frances joins her team as they present a research development with Mark about how they can reduce misinformation by 38% with only a 1% decline in engagement, though he appears unimpressed with the information. The Civic Integrity team is subsequently dissolved. Frances later meets with Jeff again after learning that Mark wanted to emphasize MSI for things like birthdays and anniversaries by cutting back on all the brands to create more of a sense of community on the site. When she asks why he didn’t post her story, he says it’s because he doesn’t have enough evidence to back up her claims.

Frances later goes to a bar where she tries to bring up her concerns to fellow teammate Morgan (Anna Lambe), but she urges Frances to drop it. On her way out, Frances also overhears a little girl is dealing with cyberbullying, and after telling her family what she does, the girl’s father asks Frances about getting the bullying pages taken down.

In another private meeting, Frances gives more info to Jeff on how the higher-ups at Facebook expressed concerns about engagement going down as users got older, which sparked a need for MSI. The COVID-19 pandemic is also in the early stages at this point, so Frances relocates to Puerto Rico because of her celiac disease. Jeff then gets Evelyn to go undercover with a fake profile to try and see how long it takes for her to get radicalized, then gives the rest of his info to his bosses.

Another jump to 2021 shows Raya still coaching Mark, but his interactions with Charlie get more heated since he is criticizing Mark for allowing misinformation to spread on the site from certain public figures.

Back in 2020, Jeff flies to Puerto Rico to keep working with Frances. He tells her he needs written proof of Facebook radicalizing its users before he starts writing his article. Later, Frances’s bosses make her return to the Bay Area because they tell her she cannot work remotely. Fearing that her identity will be compromised, she makes it clear to Jeff that she cannot risk her job anymore and cuts off contact with him.

Part Three: We’re Gonna Get Blamed For This
Frances is later visited by Morgan, who has found out that she is working with Jeff and the Wall Street Journal. Although Frances fears she will be exposed, Morgan provides her with a drive with more data on a study that shows 32% of teenage girls are negatively influenced about body issues because of the site. Frances reunites with Jeff to discuss how Mark chose to prioritize amplifying pieces of information that would emotionally charge the site’s users and make them angrier. When Raya (in a flashback) pushed back against it, Mark just said they are a “cork board” and can’t control what information gets posted.

Back in the 2021 segment, Mark and the others are aware of the information spread by Jeff. As things get more volatile between Mark and Charlie, the team is pulled away in the wake of the Capitol insurrection in D.C. Kayleigh is also shown among the rioters. As sitting President Donald Trump is encouraging his voters to engage in this, Mark takes a while before telling his team to shut down Trump’s posts.
2020 – Jeff introduces Frances to the interns and his bosses. She reluctantly plans to get whistleblower protection by testifying to Congress.

2021 – In the aftermath, Jeff has a meeting with Teddy before going ahead and publishing “The Facebook Files”. Teddy tells Jeff that he ruined Frances’s life by helping her go public, though Jeff believes she will be fine.

On the day of Frances’s testimony, Jeff goes to see her and give her a brief pep talk. Frances testifies before the Senate, and later parts ways with Jeff, raising her fist up in triumph as he smiles.

The ending text states how the Wall Street Journal posted “The Facebook Files”, which came out to 17 pages. In addition to the United States Senate, Frances Haugen also testified before U.K. Parliament, E.U. Parliament, the French National Assembly, and appeared on 60 Minutes and the cover of Time Magazine. In the wake of her testimony, 47 attorneys general filed lawsuits against Meta (Facebook’s rebrand) while the information on Instagram was more than enough for many parents to come forward. Jeff Horwitz won a Pulitzer for his coverage on social media. Meta revisited its fact-checking policy and just doesn’t fact-check at all anymore. 43% of adults get their news from Facebook.

wiki_plot.text:
In 2019, data engineer Frances Haugen joins the Civic Integrity team at Facebook. Although she believes in Facebook's mission to connect people, she discovers that its leadership prioritizes engagement and revenue over user safety. Facebook media relations executive Teddy Marks briefs employees on journalists' efforts to obtain internal information. Frances attempts to raise her concerns publicly, but the forum ends before she can speak while her colleagues dismiss her.

The Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz joins the paper's San Francisco Bureau and receives an assignment covering Facebook. A political reporter by trade, Jeff is skeptical of Facebook's influence on American life. He contacts Civic Integrity employees through LinkedIn and eventually connects with Frances, who agrees to meet despite fearing the consequences of violating her non-disclosure agreement. During their meeting, Frances describes her concerns and recounts how her friend Kayleigh, a political progressive, became radicalized after spending considerable time on Facebook and was eventually arrested for harassing concerned officers while drunk. Although interested in her allegations, Jeff lacks sufficient evidence to publish a story.

Frances accompanies her colleagues to present their findings to Mark Zuckerberg. The team explains that Facebook's algorithms amplify hate speech and divisive content, but Mark rejects their proposed changes and ends the presentation early. Fearing that Civic Integrity will be disbanded, Frances becomes more willing to share internal documents with Jeff, meeting him at his hotel. Following the 2020 United States presidential election, Facebook dissolves Civic Integrity. At a farewell party, Frances asks her colleague Morgan to sign an open letter she has written, but Morgan urges her to delete it. Morgan later visits Frances's apartment and gives her a flash drive containing an internal study of Facebook's effects on teen mental health.

Frances, who has coeliac disease, temporarily relocates to San Juan, Puerto Rico, as the COVID-19 pandemic begins. Jeff travels there to continue working with her and, armed with sufficient documentation, starts publishing articles in the Facebook Files series. Facebook's human resources department subsequently orders Frances back to the Bay Area, determining that she cannot work remotely from a U.S. territory. Fearing that Facebook will identify her as the source of the leaks, Frances cuts off contact with Jeff.

In 2021, Mark prepares to testify before the United States Senate with assistance from crisis management consultant Raya, former Facebook investor Charlie Garrigan, and several aides. Raya coaches him on questions concerning content moderation and Facebook's influence on American elections. Charlie challenges the company's approach to free speech and its fact-checking of political advertisements, while Mark maintains that Facebook operates as a "public square."

Their preparations are interrupted by news of the January 6 United States Capitol attack. After President Donald Trump fails to call off the protesters, advisers urge Mark to ban him from Facebook. Mark initially freezes but, under pressure from Raya and Charlie, ultimately decides to block Trump from posting on Facebook's platforms.

After meeting with Jeff and his colleagues, Frances resolves to seek whistleblower protection and testify before the Senate. As Jeff's reporting reaches Mark and his team, Jeff interviews Teddy on background before publishing another installment of the Facebook Files. Frances and Jeff meet in Washington, D.C., before her testimony. After delivering her opening statement, Frances shares a moment of recognition with Jeff.

Closing titles reveal that Facebook eliminated its fact-checking programs, the company changed its name to Meta in October 2021, and 43% of Americans continue to receive their news from Facebook.

reviews.text:
Racism has long been deeply rooted in American institutions, and the military is certainly no exception. The history of racial discrimination within the US armed forces is well documented, and Soul Patrol offers another disturbing reminder of the contradictions faced by Black Americans sent overseas to fight for a country that denied them equal rights at home.
J.M. Harper's documentary tells the story of the first al…

I found myself thoroughly engrossed in J.M. Harper’s SOUL PATROL, which threads together reenactments and firsthand testimony to revisit the Vietnam War’s first Black special operations team decades later. The narrative structure is evocative and highly engaging, bringing long-forgotten memories to life through these striking reenactments and stirring, very intimate moments at the soldiers’ reunion. Both approaches a…

the archival footage here (especially the 8mm footage presumably shot by soldiers) is incredible and the interviews contextualize it nicely, the two together working well to establish a people and a time and place — but the reenactments squander that momentum and humanity, would love to see a version of this without those, especially when everything else is so powerful

In J.M. Harper’s excessively rendered yet poignant Vietnam War documentary, the Black men of the F-51st gather one last time to share their collective past. They were the conflict’s first all-Black Long Range Reconnaissance team, earning the nickname Soul Patrol. That moniker became the title of Ed Emanuel’s memoir, which chronicles his and his comrade’s arduous experiences. 
At times, “Soul Patrol” can be a harrowin…

Here is the remarkable story of the US army’s “soul patrol” unit in the Vietnam war: the all-black Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol (or “LURP”) — a six-man team of largely teenage African-American soldiers, within Company F, 51st Infantry, whose duty was to go behind the Viet Cong enemy lines, each carrying one hundred and fifty pounds of kit and an M16 assault rifle, and in conditions of terrifying danger report on …

No, it’s still not the right time to celebrate people who committed war crimes in Vietnam. This is high-gloss US military propaganda.
It presents some context about what led these soldiers to join the military, but doesn’t spend nearly enough critically examining their role in the absolute horrors the U.S. military, through men like this, subjected the Vietnamese people to. I was hoping for something more complex and…
